title: The Gradual Decline of Effective Teacher Modelling - Why Tech Can Often Hinder Modelling ch-can-often-hinder-modelling/
author: Emma Turner
summary: Emma Turner argues that live teacher modelling - once the central, unavoidable act of teaching before digital resources dominated classrooms - is quietly dying, displaced by pre-prepared, clickable PowerPoint slides. Drawing on her work observing hundreds of lessons across many schools, she describes a recurring pause when she asks teachers 'how are we going to model this?', evidence that modelling has become an afterthought relative to retrieval and checking-for-understanding techniques that assume pupils already have something to retrieve. She contrasts pre-tech 'analogue' modelling - large-scale, real-time drawing, annotation, and narration - with today's static slide decks, arguing that the former harnesses spatial thinking, gesture, and slower processing time in ways screens cannot replicate. Turner frames modelling as inseparable from assessment: it is simultaneously how teachers make expert thinking visible and how they check on pupils' developing understanding. Her central warning is that without deliberate, well-modelled input, techniques like retrieval practice have nothing to draw on - you cannot retrieve what was never modelled in the first place.
points: Turner's central claim: teacher modelling is a dying art, crowded out by the efficiency of pre-prepared digital slides, even though it remains the essential bridge between curriculum design and pupil understanding.

Live, large-scale 'analogue' modelling (drawing, annotating, narrating in real time) engages spatial thinking, gesture, and slower processing time in ways that static PowerPoint slides cannot replicate.

Modelling is under-emphasised in CPD relative to retrieval-practice and checking-for-understanding techniques, even though those techniques presuppose that pupils already have something worth retrieving - which only good modelling provides.

Turner ties modelling directly to subject knowledge and assessment: expert modelling requires knowing where misconceptions lie, and it doubles as a real-time check on pupils' developing expertise, not merely an act of telling.
Her closing image - 'you can't fish in an empty lake' - crystallises the argument that retrieval strategies are hollow without the foundational, deliberately modelled content for pupils to draw upon.
quotes: Modelling is a dying art. And modelling is where the magic lies. Modelling is the bridge between excellently designed curriculum resources and what subsequently goes on in our pupils' heads.
As I visit classrooms, talk to children and teachers, and work with teams on their curriculum design and pedagogy there is frequently a pause when I say, "So how are we going to model this?
Teachers had to draw, annotate, explain, unpack and reveal in real time exactly how a text or process or diagram or idea worked.
It was also slower, and slow modelling is not a bad thing. The pace of analogue modelling allows for greater processing time for both teacher and pupil.
Modelling is not simply making expert thinking visible; it's where we check on the developing expertise of our children.

You can't fish in an empty lake, so you cannot retrieve what you don't know. Modelling is the bridge to that lake and in its deployment builds the cognitive connections that help children to make sense of our curriculum content.
